quiz.q: Why do almost all `std::fs` functions return a `Result`?
options: Because file access can always fail (missing file, no permission, full disk)
To make the code longer on purpose
quiz.explain: The filesystem is the unreliable outside world. Any read or write can fail, so the API returns a Result and forces you to handle the failure case.

quiz.q: What does the `?` operator do on a line like `let t = fs::read_to_string(p)?;`?
options: Unwraps the Ok value, or returns the Err from the current function
quiz.explain: `?` gives you the value on success, or immediately returns the error to the caller on failure — but only inside a function that itself returns Result or Option.

quiz.q: What does `fs::write("log.txt", data)` do if the file already exists?
options: Appends the data to the end
Overwrites the file completely, erasing the old contents
Returns an error and does nothing
quiz.explain: `fs::write` replaces the entire file. To add to an existing file instead, open it with `OpenOptions::new().append(true)`.

quiz.q: Which requirement must a function meet to use the `?` operator inside it?
quiz.explain: `?` needs somewhere to send an error, so the enclosing function must return a Result or Option. That's why file-reading helpers usually return `Result<String, io::Error>`.

flashcards.front: Read an entire text file into a String?
Write a string to a file (creating/overwriting it)?
flashcards.back: `std::fs::write(path, data)` — returns a Result; it overwrites any existing file.

flashcards.front: Add to a file without erasing it?
flashcards.back: Open it with `OpenOptions::new().create(true).append(true).open(path)`, then write to it.

flashcards.front: Why prefer `?` over `.unwrap()` in real programs?
flashcards.back: `.unwrap()`/`.expect()` crash the whole program on the first error; `?` propagates the error so it can be handled gracefully.
